documentation.range:
Saimiri oerstedii occurs along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panama inland. The northeastern limit is marked by the Río Tulín in the north Herradura Mountains (9°40’N, 84°35’W) and Dota Mountains (9°37’N, 84°35’W). Along the coast of the Golfo Dulce and the Burica Peninsula to the western part of the Chiriquí Province, mouth of the Río Fonseca, including the Archipelago of the Golfo de Chiriquí, in Panama (Hershkovitz 1984, Boinski et al. 1998, Reid 1997). This species has an extent of occurrence (EOO) around 24,000 km², within which its range is severely fragmented. Ceballos et al. (2019) reports a 60% decrease in the squirrel monkey's EOO and area of occupancy (AOO)over the last 20 years.

There are two subspecies: S. o. oerstedii and S. o. citrinellus. Saimiri oerstedii oerstedii occurs along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, from the left bank of the Río Grande de Térraba to the Osa Peninsula, along the coast of the Golfo Dulce and the Burica Peninsula to the western part of the Chiriquí Province, mouth of the Río Fonseca, including the Archipelago of the Golfo de Chiriquí, in Panama (Hershkovitz 1984, Boinski et al. 1998, Reid 1997). Surveys by Baldwin and Baldwin (1972, 1976) recorded its presence on the Burica Peninsula, but indicated that it is now restricted to a narrow strip of scattered lowland coastal forest fragments, not extending to the type locality David, although it possibly occurred as far east as Remedios (well to the east of David) prior to the 1950s. Altitudinal range is 0 to 500 m asl (Hershkovitz 1984). Rodríguez-Vargas (2003) mapped the remaining populations in Panama.

The historic range of S. o. citrinellus is along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, to altitudes of up to 500 m asl. The north-eastern limit is marked by the Río Tulín in the north Herradura Mountains (9°40’N, 84°35’W) and Dota Mountains (9°37’N, 84°35’W), and the southern limit is the north bank of the Río Grande de Térraba (8°25´N, 84°25´W) (Arauz 1993, Sierra et al. 2003). Its occurrence is sporadic, and the surviving populations are entirely fragmented (Alfaro 1987, Wong 1990, Sierra et al. 2003).

In recent years several surveys have indicated that squirrel monkeys are occurring in higher altitudes. Some researchers have found S. o. oerstedii from 600 to 800 m asl (Daily et al. 2003 and Morera 2007). Also, there has being reports by inhabitants of the countryside reporting squirrel monkeys at altitudes near 1200 m.a.s.l. near the Dota Mountains (Solano-Rojas 2020, pers. obs.), and in 2015, researchers reported new locations in previously unrecorded sites and at a record altitude of 1,145 m asl (Ceballos et. al. 2019).
documentation.population:
Mitchell et al. (1991) recorded a population density of 36 individuals/km² in Costa Rica; Baldwin and Baldwin (1981) recorded 130 individuals/km² in Panama.

There is some dispute by different teams as to total numbers of S. o. citrinellus. The larger estimate is 1,300–1,800 individuals (Wong 1990, Sierra et al. 2003, but see Boinski et al. 1998). This estimate was made based on 35% of their range, so the total number of individuals should be even bigger than what was estimated in previous years (Sierra et al. 2003). For the total numbers of S. o. oerstedii, researchers have suggested the total number for Costa Rica is 3,000 individuals (Boinski and Sirot 1997). More recent studies indicate at least 1,638 individuals in 54 groups only in a small portion of their range in La Amistad International Park southern limit, comprising 21,397 ha, and Rodríguez-Vargas (2003) estimates around 4,755 individuals remain in Chiriqui Peninsula in southwest Panama.

Solano-Rojas (2020, pers. obs.) found an average of 31 individuals per troop for S. o. oerstedii based on interviews to landowners outside protected areas, which means an increase of individuals per troop since earlier studies when Solano-Rojas (2007) reported an average of 19.3 individuals per troop.
It is suspected that populations have declined by at least 50% over the last three generations, due in large part to a ca 60% decline in the EOO and AOO over that time period (Ceballos et al. 2019).
documentation.habitats:
This species typically prefers seasonally inundated forests, river edge forest, floodplain, and secondary forests (see Boinski 1987c). They use all levels of the forest, but forage and travel mainly in the lower canopy and understorey. Locomotion involves predominantly quadrupedal walking and running

Squirrel monkeys are small frugivore-insectivores. They spend 75-80% of their day foraging for insects and other small animal prey (Mittermeier and Van Roosmalen 1981, Terborgh 1983, Boinski 1988). During dry season shortages of appropriate fruiting trees, they are able to depend entirely on animal prey (Janson and Boinski 1992).

Saimiri groups are multi-male and can be large, up to 100 animals (larger groups are believed to be temporary mergers of two) but most frequently are of 20-75 individuals (Baldwin and Baldwin 1981, Terborgh 1983, Mitchell et al. 1991, Solano-Rojas  2007, 2020). As emphasized by Boinski (1999a,b, 2005, Boinski et al. 2005a,b) although all squirrel monkeys are morphologically very similar, their social systems are quite distinct (summarized in Sussman 2000).

In S. oerstedii, females do not form dominance hierarchies, and there is no evidence of coalition formation in social interactions. Females transfer between groups before first mating season, and males are philopatric. There is little competition or agonistic interactions between groups, and males show high levels of vigilance for predators. Reproductively mature males collaborate in mobbing females during the mating season. The fruits they typically exploit occur in small and very scarce patches, and feeding competition is very low.

Mating and births in Saimiri are highly seasonal, seldom exceeding two months in duration (see Boinski 1987a,b). The peak of births normally occurring in February (Solano-Rojas 2007, Solano-Rojas,2020)  Single offspring, with interbirth intervals of about 12 months (Boinski 1999b). Mating usually occurs during the wet season. In S. oerstedii, sexual receptivity in females is synchronized, and lasts only one or two days each season. In S. sciureus, birth synchrony is less pronounced and births occur only once every two years.

Size:
Weight: Adult male 750–950 g (mean 829 g), adult female more than 600–800 g (mean 695 g) (Jack 2007).
documentation.threats:
The major threat to this species across its range is habitat loss, primarily due to agriculture and logging. In Panama, some specific threats are deforestation for farming, cattle ranching, teak plantations, palm oil plantations, urban investments, hydroelectric and other industrial activities. Other threats are the use of herbicides and live capture for the pet trade (Miranda-Jiménez and Méndez-Carvajal 2012a). In Costa Rica, Solano (2007) reported five main threats to the conservation of Squirrel Monkeys besides forest fragmentation and habitat loss:
  1. Crops such as maize (Zea mays), bananas (Musa spp.) and lychees (Nephelium lappaceum), due to the local inhabitants considering the monkeys a pest and then acting accordingly;
  2. Exotic plantations such as palm oil (Elais guineensis) and teak and grey teak (Tectona grandis and Gmelina arborea); (note: the teak plantations are a threat as it is cut down and then squirrel monkeys can't connect to other areas)
  3. Pet trade, this is not very common in the whole range for this subspecies and more common in the border with Panama, but some rescue centres report new arrivals on the birth season apparently from captured monkeys;
  4.  Electrical wires, there are several spots where monkeys are found dead due to electrical wires contact;
  5. Hunting dogs, and dogs in general, some dead squirrel monkeys were reported attacked and dead by hunting dogs and less commonly by domestic dogs unattended.  
There are also new threats as road kills mainly in the Central Pacific but also occurring in Southern Costa Rica, along with habitat fragmentation and habitat loss. In Costa Rica, the growth of palm oil plantations is competing with important habitat for the squirrel monkeys. These monkeys use mainly secondary growth forest owned by private landowners, whom can change the use of their land in any moment. These lands are mainly located outside protected areas.

documentation.rationale: This species is listed as Endangered based on a suspected reduction in population size of at least 50% over the last three generations due to decline in extent of occurrence (EOO) and hunting pressure. Its EOO and area of occupancy (AOO) have declined by ca 60% over the last 27.5 years (Ceballos et al. 2019). Its range is also severely fragmented range and there is ongoing loss of habitat.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Saimiri taxonomy follows Hershkovitz (1984) and Groves (2001, 2005). An alternative taxonomy is presented by Thorington Jr. (1985) as follows: S. sciureus sciureus (includes the forms albigena, macrodon, and ustus recognized by Hershkovitz, [1984]), S. sciureus boliviensis (includes the forms pluvialis Lönnberg, 1940 and jaburuensis Lönnberg, 1940 recognized by Hershkovitz [1987]), S. sciureus cassiquiarensis, S. sciureus oerstedii (includes the form citrinellus recognized by Hershkovitz [1984]), and S. madeirae (given as a junior synonym of S. ustus by Hershkovitz [1984]). Hernández-Camacho and Defler (1989) recognize S. sciureus caquetensis Allen 1916, given as a junior synonym of S. sciureus macrodon by Hershkovitz (1984). Costello et al. (1993) argued for the recognition of just two species: S. sciureus in South America, and S. oerstedii in Panama and Costa Rica. Boinski and Cropp (1999) using two nuclear genes (IRBP and ZFX) and one mitochondrial (D-Loop) strongly support the Hershkovitz (1984) taxonomy, advocating four distinct species: Saimiri sciureus, S. boliviensis, S. oerstedii and S. ustus.

See Rylands et al. (2006) for a discussion of the taxonomy of the Central American squirrel monkeys.
